imo-isl-2018-a1.title: Iterate a power relation
imo-isl-2018-a1.body:
Write $(*)$ for the equation. $f(x)=1$ clearly works: both sides equal $1$. We show it is the only solution.

**Step 1.** Take any $a,b\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$. Putting $x=f(a),\ y=b$ and then $x=f(b),\ y=a$ into $(*)$ gives
$$f\big(f(a)\big)^2f(b)=f\big(f(a)^2f(b)^2\big)=f\big(f(b)\big)^2f(a),$$
because the arguments $f(a)^2f(b)^2$ are the same. Hence
$$\frac{f(f(a))^2}{f(a)}=\frac{f(f(b))^2}{f(b)}\quad\text{for all }a,b,$$
so there is a constant $C\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$ with $f(f(a))^2=Cf(a)$ for all $a$, i.e.
$$\frac{f(a)}{C}=\left(\frac{f(f(a))}{C}\right)^2\qquad(1)$$

**Step 2.** Write $f^n$ for the $n$-th iterate of $f$. Applying (1) to $a,f(a),f^2(a),\dots$ we get
$$\frac{f(a)}{C}=\left(\frac{f^2(a)}{C}\right)^2=\left(\frac{f^3(a)}{C}\right)^4=\dots=\left(\frac{f^{n+1}(a)}{C}\right)^{2^n}$$
for every $n\ge1$. So the positive rational $q=f(a)/C$ is the $2^n$-th power of a positive rational for every $n$. In the prime factorisation $q=\prod p^{e_p}$ (with integer exponents $e_p$), each $e_p$ must then be divisible by $2^n$ for every $n$, so all $e_p=0$ and $q=1$. Thus $f(a)=C$ for every $a$.

**Step 3.** Substituting the constant $f\equiv C$ into $(*)$ gives $C=C^3$, so $C=1$.

Therefore $f(x)=1$ for all $x\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$. ∎

*Remark.* Over the positive reals the equation has other solutions, e.g. $f(x)=\sqrt x$; the rationality is essential.

imo-isl-2018-a3.title: Look at two consecutive elements
imo-isl-2018-a3.body:
**Reductions.** If $S$ is finite, it has only finitely many finite subsets, so only finitely many sums $\sum_{x\in F}1/x$ occur and some rational $r\in(0,1)$ is missed: (2) holds. So let $S$ be infinite.

If $S$ fails both assertions, so does $S\setminus\{1\}$. Indeed, $S\setminus\{1\}$ satisfying (1) clearly gives (1) for $S$. If $S\setminus\{1\}$ satisfies (2) with some $r<1$, then every reciprocal sum over a finite $F\subseteq S$ is either a sum over $S\setminus\{1\}$ (not equal to $r$) or $1+{}$such a sum, which is $\ge1>r$; so $S$ satisfies (2). Hence we may assume all elements exceed $1$, and write $S=\{x_1<x_2<x_3<\dots\}$ with $x_1\ge2$.

**Case A: $x_{n+1}\ge 2x_n$ for all $n$.** Then $x_n\ge 2^{n-1}x_1$, so
$$s=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{x_n}\le\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{2^{n-1}x_1}=\frac2{x_1}.$$
- If $x_1\ge3$, or $x_1=2$ and $x_{n+1}>2x_n$ for some $n$, then $s<1$, and every finite reciprocal sum is $\le s$. Any rational $r\in(s,1)$ is never attained, so (2) holds.
- Otherwise $x_n=2^n$ for all $n$. Then every finite reciprocal sum is a fraction with a power of $2$ as denominator, so it never equals $r=\frac13$: (2) holds.

**Case B: $x_{n+1}<2x_n$ for some $n$.** Put
$$r=\frac1{x_n}-\frac1{x_{n+1}}.$$
Then $r>0$, and $r<\frac1{x_{n+1}}$ because $\frac1{x_n}<\frac2{x_{n+1}}$; in particular $r<1$ is a positive rational. If no finite $F\subseteq S$ has $\sum_{x\in F}1/x=r$, then (2) holds. Otherwise let $r=\sum_{x\in F_0}1/x$. Since $r<1/x_{n+1}$, the element $x_{n+1}$ is not in $F_0$, so
$$\sum_{x\in F_0\cup\{x_{n+1}\}}\frac1x=r+\frac1{x_{n+1}}=\frac1{x_n}.$$
The sets $F=F_0\cup\{x_{n+1}\}$ and $G=\{x_n\}$ are distinct finite subsets of $S$ (only $F$ contains $x_{n+1}$) with equal reciprocal sums, so (1) holds. ∎

imo-isl-2018-a3.title: Parity of membership (indirect)
imo-isl-2018-a3.body:
Suppose $S$ satisfies neither assertion. Allow the empty sum $0$; since no nonempty set has reciprocal sum $0$, failure of (1) and (2) means: for every rational $r\in[0,1)$ there is a **unique** finite $F_r\subseteq S$ with $\sum_{x\in F_r}1/x=r$.

**Lemma.** If $x\in S$ and $q,r\in[0,1)$ are rational with $q-r=1/x$, then $x\in F_q$ if and only if $x\notin F_r$.

*Proof.* If $x\in F_q$, then $F_q\setminus\{x\}$ has sum $q-1/x=r$, so by uniqueness $F_r=F_q\setminus\{x\}$, which does not contain $x$. If $x\notin F_r$, then $F_r\cup\{x\}$ has sum $r+1/x=q$, so $F_q=F_r\cup\{x\}\ni x$. $\square$

Now fix $x\in S$ and a rational $r\in(0,1)$; let $n=\lfloor rx\rfloor$. The numbers $r-k/x$ ($k=0,\dots,n$) are rationals in $[0,1)$. Since $0\le r-n/x<1/x$, the set $F_{r-n/x}$ cannot contain $x$. Applying the lemma repeatedly, membership of $x$ alternates as $k$ goes from $n$ down to $0$, so
$$x\in F_r\iff \lfloor rx\rfloor\text{ is odd}.$$

Apply this with $r=\frac23$. For every $x\in F_{2/3}$, $\lfloor 2x/3\rfloor$ is odd; in particular $2x/3$ is not an integer (if it were, $3\mid x$ and $2x/3$ would be even). As $F_{2/3}$ is finite, we can choose a small rational $\varepsilon>0$ with $\lfloor(\frac23-\varepsilon)x\rfloor=\lfloor\frac{2x}3\rfloor$ for all $x\in F_{2/3}$. Then every $x\in F_{2/3}$ also lies in $F_{2/3-\varepsilon}$, so
$$\frac23-\varepsilon=\sum_{x\in F_{2/3-\varepsilon}}\frac1x\ge\sum_{x\in F_{2/3}}\frac1x=\frac23,$$
a contradiction. ∎

imo-isl-2018-a4.title: Shrinking range of possible values
imo-isl-2018-a4.body:
**Answer: $\dfrac{2016}{2017^2}$.**

**The value is attained.** Take $a_1=\dots=a_{2016}=1$ (each with $k=1$), then
$$a_{2017}=\frac{a_{2016}+\dots+a_0}{2017}=1-\frac1{2017},\qquad a_{2018}=\frac{a_{2017}+\dots+a_1}{2017}=1-\frac1{2017^2},$$
so $a_{2018}-a_{2017}=\frac1{2017}-\frac1{2017^2}=\frac{2016}{2017^2}$.

**Upper bound.** Write $S(n,k)=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots+a_{n-k}$ for $0\le k\le n$ (so $S(n,0)=0$, $S(n,1)=a_{n-1}$). For $n\ge1$ let
$$M_n=\max_{1\le k\le n}\frac{S(n,k)}k,\qquad m_n=\min_{1\le k\le n}\frac{S(n,k)}k,\qquad \Delta_n=M_n-m_n\ge0.$$
For $n\ge2$ we have $a_n\in[m_n,M_n]$, and also $a_{n-1}=S(n,1)/1\in[m_n,M_n]$. Hence $a_{2018}-a_{2017}\le\Delta_{2018}$. Note also $km_n\le S(n,k)\le kM_n$ for $0\le k\le n$.

**Claim.** For $n>2$, $\Delta_n\le\frac{n-1}n\Delta_{n-1}$.

*Proof.* Pick $k,\ell\le n$ with $M_n=S(n,k)/k$ and $m_n=S(n,\ell)/\ell$. Since $S(n,k)=a_{n-1}+S(n-1,k-1)$ and $S(n-1,k-1)\le(k-1)M_{n-1}$,
$$k(M_n-a_{n-1})=S(n-1,k-1)-(k-1)a_{n-1}\le(k-1)(M_{n-1}-a_{n-1}).$$
Similarly $\ell(a_{n-1}-m_n)\le(\ell-1)(a_{n-1}-m_{n-1})$. As $m_{n-1}\le a_{n-1}\le M_{n-1}$ and $\frac{k-1}k,\frac{\ell-1}\ell\le\frac{n-1}n$,
$$\Delta_n=(M_n-a_{n-1})+(a_{n-1}-m_n)\le\frac{n-1}n\big((M_{n-1}-a_{n-1})+(a_{n-1}-m_{n-1})\big)=\frac{n-1}n\Delta_{n-1}.\ \square$$

By induction every $a_n$ ($n\ge0$) lies in $[0,1]$, being an average of earlier terms. If $a_n=1$ for all $1\le n\le2017$, then $a_{2018}\le1$ and $a_{2018}-a_{2017}\le0$. Otherwise let $q$ ($2\le q\le2017$) be the least index with $a_q<1$. Then $S(q,i)=i$ for $i<q$ and $S(q,q)=q-1$, so $a_q<1$ forces $a_q=S(q,q)/q=1-\frac1q$. Consequently $S(q+1,i)=i-\frac1q$ for $1\le i\le q$ and $S(q+1,q+1)=q-\frac1q$. The ratios $S(q+1,i)/i=1-\frac1{qi}$ increase with $i\le q$, and $S(q+1,q+1)/(q+1)=\frac{q-1}q$, so
$$m_{q+1}=\frac{q-1}q,\qquad M_{q+1}=\frac{S(q+1,q)}q=\frac{q^2-1}{q^2},\qquad \Delta_{q+1}=\frac{q-1}{q^2}.$$
With $N=2017\ge q$, applying the claim for $n=q+2,\dots,N+1$:
$$\Delta_{N+1}\le\frac{q-1}{q^2}\cdot\frac{q+1}{q+2}\cdot\frac{q+2}{q+3}\cdots\frac{N}{N+1}=\frac1{N+1}\Big(1-\frac1{q^2}\Big)\le\frac1{N+1}\Big(1-\frac1{N^2}\Big)=\frac{N-1}{N^2}.$$
So $a_{2018}-a_{2017}\le\frac{2016}{2017^2}$, and the maximum is $\dfrac{2016}{2017^2}$.

imo-isl-2018-a5.title: Eliminate with four substitutions
imo-isl-2018-a5.body:
Call the equation (1).

**These functions work.** For $f(t)=C_1t+\frac{C_2}t$:
$$\Big(x+\frac1x\Big)\Big(C_1y+\frac{C_2}y\Big)=\Big(C_1xy+\frac{C_2}{xy}\Big)+\Big(C_1\frac yx+C_2\frac xy\Big)=f(xy)+f\Big(\frac yx\Big).$$

**No others.** Fix $a>1$ (say $a=2$) and let $t>0$ be arbitrary. Substituting into (1):
- $x=y=t$: $\big(t+\frac1t\big)f(t)=f(t^2)+f(1)$;
- $x=\frac ta,\ y=at$: $\big(\frac ta+\frac at\big)f(at)=f(t^2)+f(a^2)$;
- $x=a^2t,\ y=t$: $\big(a^2t+\frac1{a^2t}\big)f(t)=f(a^2t^2)+f\big(\frac1{a^2}\big)$;
- $x=y=at$: $\big(at+\frac1{at}\big)f(at)=f(a^2t^2)+f(1)$.

Subtracting the second from the first and the fourth from the third eliminates $f(t^2)$ and $f(a^2t^2)$:
$$\Big(t+\frac1t\Big)f(t)-\Big(\frac ta+\frac at\Big)f(at)=f(1)-f(a^2),$$
$$\Big(a^2t+\frac1{a^2t}\Big)f(t)-\Big(at+\frac1{at}\Big)f(at)=f\big(\tfrac1{a^2}\big)-f(1).$$
Multiply the first by $\big(at+\frac1{at}\big)$, the second by $\big(\frac ta+\frac at\big)$ and subtract, eliminating $f(at)$:
$$D\cdot f(t)=\Big(at+\frac1{at}\Big)\big(f(1)-f(a^2)\big)-\Big(\frac ta+\frac at\Big)\big(f(\tfrac1{a^2})-f(1)\big),$$
where, after expanding,
$$D=\Big(at+\frac1{at}\Big)\Big(t+\frac1t\Big)-\Big(\frac ta+\frac at\Big)\Big(a^2t+\frac1{a^2t}\Big)=a+\frac1a-a^3-\frac1{a^3}.$$
Since $u\mapsto u+\frac1u$ is increasing on $(1,\infty)$ and $a^3>a>1$, $D<0$; in particular $D\ne0$ and $D$ does not depend on $t$. The right-hand side has the form $\alpha t+\beta/t$ with $\alpha,\beta$ depending only on $a$ and the values $f(1),f(a^2),f(1/a^2)$. Dividing by $D$ gives $f(t)=C_1t+\frac{C_2}t$ for all $t>0$, with constants $C_1,C_2$.

So the solutions are exactly $f(x)=C_1x+\frac{C_2}x$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-a6.title: Reduce to one variable with finite differences
imo-isl-2018-a6.body:
For a one-variable polynomial $p$ let $(\Delta p)(x)=p(x+1)-p(x)$; if $p$ is nonconstant then $\deg\Delta p=\deg p-1$. For a polynomial $p$ in $n$ variables let $(\Delta_1p)(x_1,\dots,x_n)=p(x_1+1,x_2,\dots,x_n)-p(x_1,\dots,x_n)$; either $\Delta_1p=0$ or $\deg\Delta_1p\le\deg p-1$ (the top-degree terms cancel).

**Lemma.** Let $a_1,\dots,a_n\ge0$ be integers and $G$ a nonzero one-variable polynomial with $\deg G\le a_1+\dots+a_n$. If a polynomial $F$ satisfies
$$F(x_1,\dots,x_n)=G(x_1+\dots+x_n)\quad\text{for all }(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\{0,\dots,a_1\}\times\dots\times\{0,\dots,a_n\},$$
then $F\ne0$ and $\deg F\ge\deg G$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\deg G$. If $G$ is a nonzero constant, $F(0,\dots,0)=G(0)\ne0$, so $F\ne0$. Now let $\deg G\ge1$; then some $a_i\ge1$, say $a_1\ge1$. Put $F_1=\Delta_1F$ and $G_1=\Delta G$. For $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\{0,\dots,a_1-1\}\times\{0,\dots,a_2\}\times\dots\times\{0,\dots,a_n\}$,
$$F_1(x_1,\dots,x_n)=G(x_1+\dots+x_n+1)-G(x_1+\dots+x_n)=G_1(x_1+\dots+x_n).$$
$G_1$ is nonzero with $\deg G_1=\deg G-1\le(a_1-1)+a_2+\dots+a_n$, so by the induction hypothesis $F_1\ne0$ and $\deg F_1\ge\deg G_1$. Since $F_1=\Delta_1F\ne0$, $\deg F\ge\deg F_1+1\ge\deg G_1+1=\deg G$. $\square$

**The problem.** Let $g$ be the unique polynomial of degree $\le n(m-1)$ with $g(x)=\lfloor x/m\rfloor$ for $x\in\{0,1,\dots,n(m-1)\}$ (there are $n(m-1)+1$ prescribed values). Since $g(0)=0$ and $g(m)=1$ (note $m\le n(m-1)$), $g$ is nonconstant; and $g(0)=g(1)=0$, $g(m)=1$ rule out degree $1$, so $\deg g\ge2$.

Apply the lemma with $a_1=\dots=a_n=m-1$, $F=f$, $G=g$: on the grid $\{0,\dots,m-1\}^n$ the sum $x_1+\dots+x_n$ lies in $\{0,\dots,n(m-1)\}$, so $f=g(x_1+\dots+x_n)$ there. Hence $\deg f\ge\deg g$.

Now let $h(x)=g(x+m)-g(x)-1$. Since $\deg g\ge2$, $\deg h=\deg g-1\ge1$, so $h\ne0$. For integers $0\le x\le n(m-1)-m$ both $x$ and $x+m$ are in the interpolation range and $\lfloor(x+m)/m\rfloor=\lfloor x/m\rfloor+1$, so $h(x)=0$. That is $n(m-1)-m+1=(n-1)(m-1)$ roots, hence
$$\deg f\ge\deg g=\deg h+1\ge(n-1)(m-1)+1\ge n,$$
using $m-1\ge1$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-a7.title: Hölder plus a tangent-line bound
imo-isl-2018-a7.body:
**Answer: $\dfrac8{\sqrt[3]7}$**, attained when $(a,b,c,d)$ is a cyclic permutation of $(1,49,1,49)$.

**Attained.** For $(1,49,1,49)$:
$$S=2\Big(\sqrt[3]{\tfrac1{56}}+\sqrt[3]{\tfrac{49}8}\Big)=2\Big(\frac1{2\sqrt[3]7}+\frac{\sqrt[3]{49}}2\Big)=\frac{1+7}{\sqrt[3]7}=\frac8{\sqrt[3]7}.$$

**Upper bound.** All sums below are cyclic over $(a,b,c,d)$. Write each term as $\sqrt[6]a\cdot\sqrt[6]a\cdot\frac1{\sqrt[3]{b+7}}$. Hölder's inequality $\big(\sum uvw\big)^3\le\sum u^3\sum v^3\sum w^3$ gives
$$S^3\le\Big(\sum\sqrt a\Big)^2\sum\frac1{b+7}.$$
Next, for $x\ge0$,
$$(x^2-16x+71)(x^2+7)-448=x^4-16x^3+78x^2-112x+49=(x-1)^2(x-7)^2\ge0,$$
so with $x=\sqrt b$: $\frac1{b+7}\le\frac{b-16\sqrt b+71}{448}$. Summing and using $\sum b=100$:
$$\sum\frac1{b+7}\le\frac{384-16\sum\sqrt b}{448}=\frac{48-2\sum\sqrt a}{56}.$$
(In particular $48-2\sum\sqrt a>0$.) With $\sigma=\sum\sqrt a$ and AM–GM on $\sigma,\sigma,48-2\sigma$:
$$S^3\le\frac1{56}\,\sigma\cdot\sigma\cdot(48-2\sigma)\le\frac1{56}\Big(\frac{\sigma+\sigma+48-2\sigma}3\Big)^3=\frac{16^3}{56}=\frac{512}7.$$
Hence $S\le\frac8{\sqrt[3]7}$, and the maximum is $\dfrac8{\sqrt[3]7}$.

imo-isl-2018-c1.title: Powers of 3
imo-isl-2018-c1.body:
Take
$$S=\{1\cdot3^k,\ 2\cdot3^k:\ k=1,2,\dots,n-1\}\cup\Big\{1,\ \frac{3^n+9}2-1\Big\}.$$

**The $2n$ elements are distinct positive integers.** The numbers $3^k,2\cdot3^k$ ($1\le k\le n-1$) are $2n-2$ distinct multiples of $3$. Since $3^n$ is odd, $\frac{3^n+9}2$ is an integer, and $\frac{3^n+9}2-1=\frac{3^n+7}2$; as $3^n+7\equiv1\pmod3$ and $2$ is invertible mod $3$, this is not divisible by $3$, and it exceeds $1$. So the last two elements are distinct from each other and from the first $2n-2$.

**Total sum.**
$$\Sigma=1+\Big(\frac{3^n+9}2-1\Big)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}3\cdot3^k=\frac{3^n+9}2+\frac{3^{n+1}-9}2=2\cdot3^n.$$
So it suffices to find, for each $m=2,\dots,n$, an $m$-element subset $A_m\subset S$ with sum $3^n$ (its complement then has the same sum).

**The subsets.** Let
$$A_m=\{2\cdot3^k:\ k=n-m+1,\dots,n-1\}\cup\{3^{n-m+1}\}.$$
Since $2\le m\le n$, the exponents $n-m+1,\dots,n-1$ lie in $[1,n-1]$, so these are $m-1$ elements of the form $2\cdot3^k$ plus one element $3^{n-m+1}$ of the form $1\cdot3^k$ — all in $S$ and distinct, so $|A_m|=m$. Its sum is
$$3^{n-m+1}+2\sum_{k=n-m+1}^{n-1}3^k=3^{n-m+1}+\big(3^n-3^{n-m+1}\big)=3^n,$$
using $2(3^a+3^{a+1}+\dots+3^{b})=3^{b+1}-3^a$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-c2.title: Black squares vs. 4-cycles
imo-isl-2018-c2.body:
**Answer: $K=100$.** (This is IMO 2018 Problem 4, there phrased with "sites" and the forbidden distance $\sqrt5$, which is exactly a knight's move.)

**Horst can place 100 knights.** Colour the board like a chessboard. A knight always moves to a square of the other colour, so knights on squares of the same colour never attack each other. Horst simply places every knight on an empty black square. Before Horst's $i$-th move exactly $2(i-1)$ squares are occupied; for $i\le100$ this is at most $198<200$, the number of black squares, so an empty black square is available. Hence Horst places at least $100$ knights.

**Queenie can prevent a 101st knight.** Split the board into twenty-five $4\times4$ blocks. In a $4\times4$ block with coordinates $1,\dots,4$, the $16$ squares split into four knight-move $4$-cycles
$$(1,1)\!-\!(2,3)\!-\!(4,4)\!-\!(3,2),\quad (1,4)\!-\!(3,3)\!-\!(4,1)\!-\!(2,2),$$
$$(1,2)\!-\!(3,1)\!-\!(4,3)\!-\!(2,4),\quad (1,3)\!-\!(2,1)\!-\!(4,2)\!-\!(3,4),$$
where consecutive squares (cyclically) are a knight's move apart (one checks each step changes the coordinates by $(\pm1,\pm2)$ or $(\pm2,\pm1)$). This partitions the board into $100$ cycles $A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D\!-\!A$, and in each cycle the "opposite" squares $A,C$ (and $B,D$) are symmetric about the centre of the block.

Queenie's strategy: whenever Horst puts a knight on a square $A$ of some cycle $A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D$, she puts her queen on the opposite square $C$.

This is always possible, and Horst gets at most one knight per cycle. Indeed, Queenie only ever plays in the cycle where Horst has just played. When Horst places the first knight of a cycle on $A$, nothing has been placed in that cycle yet, so $C$ is empty and Queenie takes it. Afterwards $A$ and $C$ are occupied, and $B$, $D$ are both attacked by the knight on $A$, so Horst can never play in this cycle again (and so Queenie never needs to either). Hence Horst places at most $100$ knights.

Therefore $K=100$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-c3.title: Label the stones
imo-isl-2018-c3.body:
The stones are indistinguishable and the outcome of each turn only depends on which square is chosen and how far a stone moves. So we may decide, at each turn, *which* stone of the chosen square is moved.

Number the stones $1,2,\dots,n$ and adopt the rule: whenever Sisyphus chooses a square, the stone with the **largest number** on that square is the one that moves. This does not change the sequence of board positions, hence not the number of turns.

Consider stone $k$. Whenever it is moved, it is the largest-numbered stone on its square, so all stones on that square have numbers $\le k$; hence the square holds at most $k$ stones, and stone $k$ moves at most $k$ squares in that turn. Stone $k$ has to travel from square $0$ to square $n$, a total distance of $n$, so it is moved in at least $\lceil n/k\rceil$ turns.

Each turn moves exactly one stone, so the total number of turns is at least
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left\lceil\frac nk\right\rceil.$$
∎

imo-isl-2018-c5.title: Bound each stay, then build an optimal schedule
imo-isl-2018-c5.body:
**Answer: $\dfrac{k(4k^2+k-1)}2$.**

Number the days $1,2,\dots,D$ with $D=\binom{2k}2$. Let $b_1\le b_2\le\dots\le b_{2k}$ be the arrival days in nondecreasing order and $e_1\ge e_2\ge\dots\ge e_{2k}$ the departure days in nonincreasing order (the $i$-th entries need not belong to the same player). A player arriving on day $b$ and leaving on day $e$ costs $e-b+1$, so the total cost is
$$\Sigma=\sum e_i-\sum b_i+2k=\sum_{i=0}^{2k-1}\big(e_{i+1}-b_{i+1}+1\big).$$

**Lower bound.** Fix $0\le i\le 2k-1$. Let $P$ be the set of days before $b_{i+1}$ and $Q$ the set of days after $e_{i+1}$. On a day in $P$ only players arriving before $b_{i+1}$ are present, and they are among the $i$ first arrivals (set $\mathcal A$, $|\mathcal A|=i$); so the match of that day is a pair inside $\mathcal A$. Likewise the match of a day in $Q$ is a pair inside the set $\mathcal D$ of the $i$ last-departing players. Each pair plays only once, so
$$|P\cup Q|\le 2\binom i2-\binom{|\mathcal A\cap\mathcal D|}2 .$$
The days outside $P\cup Q$ are exactly those in $[b_{i+1},e_{i+1}]$, so $e_{i+1}-b_{i+1}+1\ge D-|P\cup Q|$. Using $|\mathcal A\cap\mathcal D|\ge 0$ always, and $|\mathcal A\cap\mathcal D|\ge 2i-2k$ when $i>k$:
$$e_{i+1}-b_{i+1}+1\ge\begin{cases}\binom{2k}2-2\binom i2=k(2k-1)-i(i-1), & i\le k,\\[4pt] \binom{2k}2-2\binom i2+\binom{2i-2k}2=(2k-i)^2,& i>k.\end{cases}$$
(For the second line expand: $2k^2-k-i^2+i+2(i-k)^2-(i-k)=(2k-i)^2$.) Summing,
$$\Sigma\ge\sum_{i=0}^{k}\big(k(2k-1)-i(i-1)\big)+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}j^2=k(k+1)(2k-1)-\frac{(k-1)k(k+1)}3+\frac{(k-1)k(2k-1)}6=\frac{k(4k^2+k-1)}2.$$

**A schedule attaining every bound.** Split the players into $X=\{S_1,\dots,S_k\}$ and $Y=\{T_1,\dots,T_k\}$. 
1. *First part:* the players of $X$ arrive one by one; each new arrival immediately plays everybody already present.
2. *Middle part:* $T_1,T_2,\dots,T_k$ arrive in this order; on arrival $T_j$ immediately plays all $S_i$ with $i>j$. Then $S_k,S_{k-1},\dots,S_1$ leave in this order, each $S_i$ first playing all $T_j$ with $j\ge i$. (So $T_k$'s first match is with $S_k$, which is $S_k$'s last match.)
3. *Third part:* the players of $Y$ leave one by one, each playing everybody still present just before leaving.

Every pair plays exactly once: pairs in $X$ in part 1, pairs in $Y$ in part 3, and $S_iT_j$ on $T_j$'s arrival if $i>j$, before $S_i$'s departure if $i\le j$.

*Check of the bounds.* For $i\le k$ the first $i$ arrivals have played all $\binom i2$ of their matches before the next arrival, so $b_{i+1}=\binom i2+1$; symmetrically $e_{i+1}=D-\binom i2$. For $i>k$, the $(i+1)$-th arrival is $T_{i+1-k}$ and the $(i+1)$-th last departure is $S_{i+1-k}$. For $0\le s\le k-1$, the matches from $T_{k-s}$'s arrival to $S_{k-s}$'s departure are: the arrival matches of $T_{k-s},\dots,T_{k-1}$ ($1+2+\dots+s$ of them), the match $S_kT_k$, and the departure matches of $S_{k-1},\dots,S_{k-s}$ ($2+3+\dots+(s+1)$), in total $(s+1)^2$. With $s=2k-i-1$ this gives $e_{i+1}-b_{i+1}+1=(2k-i)^2$. So all bounds are equalities and the minimum cost is $\dfrac{k(4k^2+k-1)}2$.

imo-isl-2018-c6.title: Count appearances of each number
imo-isl-2018-c6.body:
If $d=\gcd(a,b)>1$, every number ever written is a multiple of $d$, and dividing everything by $d$ gives the same process for $a/d,b/d$. So assume $\gcd(a,b)=1$, and without loss of generality $a<b$.

Suppose that operation (ii) is performed infinitely often. Consider a moment at which (ii) is about to be performed and has already been performed $N$ times. For each integer $k$ let $f(k)$ be the number of times the number $k$ has been written on the board so far (as a new $0$ or as the result of an increase). Then $f(0)=2N$ (zeros are only produced by (ii)), $f(k)=0$ for $k<0$, and only finitely many $f(k)$ are nonzero.

**Recursion.** At this moment no two equal numbers are on the board, so at most one copy of each $k$ is present. Every copy of $k$ that disappeared did so in a move (i) applied to a pair of copies of $k$; so the number of moves applied to the value $k$ is $\big(f(k)-\varepsilon_k\big)/2=\lfloor f(k)/2\rfloor$, where $\varepsilon_k\in\{0,1\}$ is the number of copies of $k$ now on the board (it has the parity of $f(k)$). Each such move creates one $k+a$ and one $k+b$, and a number $k\ge1$ arises only in this way (from $k-a$ or $k-b$, which are different as $a\ne b$). Hence
$$f(k)=\Big\lfloor\frac{f(k-a)}2\Big\rfloor+\Big\lfloor\frac{f(k-b)}2\Big\rfloor\quad(k\ge1),\qquad\text{so}\qquad f(k)\ge\frac{f(k-a)+f(k-b)}2-1.\qquad(1)$$

**Claim.** If $x=sa+tb$ with integers $s,t\ge0$, then $f(x)>\dfrac{f(0)}{2^{s+t}}-2$.

*Proof by induction on $s+t$.* For $s+t=0$, $x=0$ and this is clear. If $s+t\ge1$, say $s\ge1$ (the case $t\ge1$ is symmetric), then $x\ge1$ and by (1), using $f(x-b)\ge0$ and the induction hypothesis for $x-a=(s-1)a+tb$,
$$f(x)\ge\frac{f(x-a)}2-1>\frac12\Big(\frac{f(0)}{2^{s+t-1}}-2\Big)-1=\frac{f(0)}{2^{s+t}}-2.\ \square$$

**Contradiction.** Let $n=ab-a-b$. Each of $n+1,\dots,n+b$ can be written as $sa+tb$ with $0\le s\le b-1$ and $t\ge0$ (as $\gcd(a,b)=1$, choose $s\equiv xa^{-1}\pmod b$; then $x-sa\ge n+1-(b-1)a=1-b>-b$ is a multiple of $b$, hence $\ge0$), and then $tb\le n+b=ab-a<ab$, so $t\le a-1$. Thus $s+t\le a+b$. Since (ii) happens infinitely often, we can choose the moment so that $N\ge2^{a+b+1}$, i.e. $f(0)\ge2^{a+b+2}$. The claim then gives $f(n+j)>4-2=2$, so $f(n+j)\ge2$ for $j=1,\dots,b$.

Now by (1), for $j>b$: $f(n+j)=\lfloor f(n+j-a)/2\rfloor+\lfloor f(n+j-b)/2\rfloor\ge1+1=2$ whenever $f(n+j-a),f(n+j-b)\ge2$; since $n+j-a,\ n+j-b\ge n+1$, induction on $j$ gives $f(n+j)\ge2$ for all $j\ge1$. So infinitely many different numbers have been written after finitely many moves — impossible.

Hence (ii) is performed only finitely many times. ∎

imo-isl-2018-c7.title: Two parity lemmas, then Euler's formula
imo-isl-2018-c7.body:
Let $n=2018$. Each circle meets the other $n-1$ circles in $2$ points each, so it carries $2n-2$ vertices. For a vertex $v$ on circle $C$ write $c_C(v)$ for the colour $v$ gets from $C$; $v=C\cap C'$ is yellow iff $c_C(v)\ne c_{C'}(v)$. On one circle, two vertices get the same colour iff the number of vertices strictly between them on an arc is odd. Note also: the two arcs of a circle between two of its vertices contain numbers of interior vertices with the same parity (they add to $2n-4$).

**Lemma 1.** If circles $C,C'$ cross at $x$ and $y$, then $x,y$ are both yellow or both non-yellow.

*Proof.* Let $\alpha\subset C$ and $\beta\subset C'$ be arcs from $x$ to $y$. Any other circle $E$ avoids $x,y$, and walking along $\alpha$ each crossing with $E$ toggles inside/outside of $E$; so $|E\cap\alpha|\equiv[x,y\text{ on different sides of }E]\equiv|E\cap\beta|\pmod 2$. Summing over $E$, the numbers of interior vertices of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have the same parity $p$. If $p$ is odd, $c_C(x)=c_C(y)$ and $c_{C'}(x)=c_{C'}(y)$; if $p$ is even, both colours switch from $x$ to $y$. Either way, $c_C(x)\ne c_{C'}(x)\iff c_C(y)\ne c_{C'}(y)$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** Let $C_1,C_2,C_3$ be distinct circles, $x\in C_2\cap C_3$, $y\in C_3\cap C_1$, $z\in C_1\cap C_2$. Then an odd number of $x,y,z$ are yellow.

*Proof.* Let $\alpha_1\subset C_1$ go from $y$ to $z$, $\alpha_2\subset C_2$ from $z$ to $x$, $\alpha_3\subset C_3$ from $x$ to $y$, with $k_1,k_2,k_3$ interior vertices. The six colours satisfy: $c_1(y)\ne c_1(z)$ iff $k_1$ even, etc. Going around the cycle $c_1(z),c_1(y),c_3(y),c_3(x),c_2(x),c_2(z),c_1(z)$ the number of colour changes is even; the changes along arcs number $\equiv 3-(k_1+k_2+k_3)$, and those at corners are the yellow corners. So it suffices to show $k_1+k_2+k_3$ is even. By the remark above we may replace any $\alpha_i$ by the complementary arc, so take every $\alpha_i$ to be traversed **counterclockwise** in the stated direction.

*(a) Other circles.* A circle $E\notin\{C_1,C_2,C_3\}$ meets $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ in $\equiv[y,z\text{ differ}]+[z,x\text{ differ}]+[x,y\text{ differ}]\equiv0$ points (sides of $E$).

*(b) The circles themselves.* Let $x',y',z'$ be the second intersection points of $C_2C_3$, $C_3C_1$, $C_1C_2$. On $\alpha_1$, the only possible interior crossings with $C_3$ and $C_2$ are $y'$ and $z'$. Walking along $\alpha_1$ from $y$ (on $C_3$) to $z$, crossings with $C_3$ toggle the side of $C_3$, so $[y'\in\alpha_1]\equiv[\alpha_1\text{ starts into the disc of }C_3]+[z\text{ inside }C_3]$; similarly $[z'\in\alpha_1]\equiv[\alpha_1\text{ ends at }z\text{ from inside }C_2]+[y\text{ inside }C_2]$. Doing the same for $\alpha_2,\alpha_3$, each "point" term such as $[z\text{ inside }C_3]$ appears twice (from $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$) and cancels. What remains are two direction terms at each corner; at $z$ they are $[\alpha_1\text{ arrives inside }C_2]+[\alpha_2\text{ leaves into }C_1]$.

*(c) Local fact.* At a crossing $p$ of circles $C,C'$ with outward unit normals $\mathbf n,\mathbf n'$ and $J$ the rotation by $+90^\circ$: moving clockwise along $C$ from $p$ (direction $-J\mathbf n$) enters the disc of $C'$ iff $J\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n'>0$; moving counterclockwise along $C'$ (direction $J\mathbf n'$) enters the disc of $C$ iff $J\mathbf n'\cdot\mathbf n<0$, i.e. iff $J\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n'>0$ (as $J\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=-\mathbf a\cdot J\mathbf b$). So the two events coincide. At $z$, $\alpha_1$ run backwards leaves $z$ clockwise along $C_1$ and $\alpha_2$ leaves $z$ counterclockwise along $C_2$; so the two terms at $z$ are equal and their sum is even. The same holds at $x$ and $y$.

Thus $k_1+k_2+k_3$ is even and the lemma follows. $\square$

**Counting yellow vertices from one circle.** Let a circle $C$ carry $k$ yellow points. By Lemma 1 they are the crossing points of $C$ with a set $\mathcal Y$ of $k/2$ circles; the other $n-1-k/2$ circles (set $\mathcal N$) cross $C$ at non-yellow points. For two circles $D,D'$ both in $\mathcal Y$ (or both in $\mathcal N$), apply Lemma 2 to $C,D,D'$ with $y,z$ the corners on $C$: both corners on $C$ are yellow (both non-yellow), so each point of $D\cap D'$ is yellow. Hence the total number $Y$ of yellow vertices satisfies
$$Y\ge k+2\binom{k/2}2+2\binom{n-1-k/2}2=\frac{k^2}2-(n-2)k+(n-1)(n-2).$$

**Counting regions.** The circles form a connected plane graph with $V=n(n-1)$ vertices of degree $4$ and $E=2n(n-1)$ edges, so by Euler's formula there are $F=n(n-1)+2$ regions. The four corners at a vertex lie in four different regions (they differ in being inside/outside the two circles).

*Around a region the non-yellow vertices alternate red/blue.* Walk around the boundary: along an edge (an arc between consecutive vertices of one circle) that circle's colour flips; at a vertex the boundary switches circles, and the colour flips again exactly when the vertex is yellow. Between two consecutive non-yellow vertices with $j$ yellow ones in between, there are $j+1$ edges, giving $2j+1$ flips — odd. So consecutive non-yellow vertices have opposite colours, and every region has an even number of non-yellow vertices.

Now suppose no region has all vertices yellow. Then every region has at least $2$ non-yellow vertices; counting vertex–region incidences (each vertex has $4$), the number of non-yellow vertices is at least $2F/4=\frac{n(n-1)}2+1$, so
$$Y\le\frac{n(n-1)}2-1.$$

**Conclusion.** Combining, $\frac{k^2}2-(n-2)k+(n-1)(n-2)\le\frac{n(n-1)}2-1$, i.e. $k^2-2(n-2)k+(n-2)(n-3)\le0$, i.e. $(k-(n-2))^2\le n-2$. Hence $k\le n-2+\lfloor\sqrt{n-2}\rfloor=2016+44=2060$. So if some circle has at least $2061$ yellow points, some region has only yellow vertices. ∎

imo-isl-2018-g2.title: A circle with diameter $PZ$
imo-isl-2018-g2.body:
Since $AB=AC$, the line $AM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BC$; as $PA\parallel BC$, $\angle PAM=90^\circ$.

Let $Z$ be the intersection of line $AM$ with the line through $Y$ perpendicular to $PC$. *$Z$ lies on the ray $AM$ beyond $M$:* put $M=(0,0)$, $B=(-1,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $A=(0,h)$ with $h>0$, $P=(p,h)$ with $p<0$ (because $PB<PC$), $Z=(0,z)$, and $Y=C+\lambda(C-P)$ with $\lambda>0$. The condition $ZY\perp PC$ reads $Z\cdot(C-P)=Y\cdot(C-P)$. Here $C-P=(1-p,-h)$, so $Z\cdot(C-P)=-hz$, while $Y\cdot(C-P)=C\cdot(C-P)+\lambda|C-P|^2=(1-p)+\lambda|C-P|^2>0$. Hence $z<0$. Thus $Z$, $X$, $Y$ all lie on the opposite side of $BC$ from $P$ and $A$.

1. $\angle PAZ=\angle PYZ=90^\circ$, so $A$ and $Y$ lie on the circle $\omega$ with diameter $PZ$.
2. $\angle CMZ=\angle CYZ=90^\circ$, so $C,Y,Z,M$ lie on the circle with diameter $CZ$; as $Y,Z$ are on the same side of $CM$, $\angle CZM=\angle CYM$.
3. $\angle CYM=\angle PYM=\angle PXM=\angle BXM$ (given), and by the symmetry in the line $ZM$ (which swaps $B$ and $C$), $\angle BZM=\angle CZM$. Hence $\angle BXM=\angle BZM$ with $X,Z$ on the same side of $BM$, so $B,X,Z,M$ are concyclic.
4. In that circle $\angle BMZ=90^\circ$, so $BZ$ is a diameter and $\angle BXZ=90^\circ$; since $B$ lies on line $PX$, $\angle PXZ=90^\circ$, i.e. $X\in\omega$.

So $P,A,X,Y,Z$ all lie on $\omega$; in particular $APXY$ is cyclic. ∎

imo-isl-2018-g3.title: Fan construction and an area bound
imo-isl-2018-g3.body:
**Answer: all $t$ with $0<t\le4$.**

**Every $t\le4$ works.** We show that for each $n$ there is a good collection of $n$ triangles of perimeter $>4$. Let $BC$ be a diameter of $\omega$. We build inductively an inscribed polygon $BA_1A_2\dots A_nC$ (vertices in this order along a semicircle) such that the triangles
$$BA_1A_2,\ BA_2A_3,\ \dots,\ BA_{n-1}A_n,\ BA_nC$$
all have perimeter $>4$. These triangles form a fan triangulation of a convex polygon from the vertex $B$, so they have disjoint interiors, i.e. the collection is good.

For $n=1$ take any $A_1$ on the semicircle; $BA_1+A_1C>BC$, so the perimeter of $BA_1C$ exceeds $2BC=4$. For the step, assume $BA_1\dots A_nC$ is built. As $A_nB+A_nC+BC>4$, we can choose $A_{n+1}$ on the small arc $CA_n$ so close to $C$ that $A_nB+A_nA_{n+1}+BA_{n+1}>4$ (the left side tends to $A_nB+A_nC+BC$ as $A_{n+1}\to C$). The triangle $BA_{n+1}C$ again has perimeter $>2BC=4$, and the old triangle $BA_nC$ is replaced by $BA_nA_{n+1}$ and $BA_{n+1}C$.

**No $t>4$ works.** Write $t=4+2\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$, and suppose a good collection of $n$ triangles of perimeter $>t$ exists.

*Claim.* An inscribed triangle with perimeter $2s>4+2\varepsilon$ has area at least $\sigma=\sqrt{(2+\varepsilon)\varepsilon^3}$.

*Proof.* Its sides $a,b,c$ are chords of $\omega$, so each is at most $2$. Hence $s-a>(2+\varepsilon)-2=\varepsilon$, and likewise $s-b,s-c>\varepsilon$. By Heron's formula the area is $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}\ge\sqrt{(2+\varepsilon)\varepsilon^3}$. $\square$

The triangles have disjoint interiors and lie in the disc of area $\pi$, so $n\sigma\le\pi$. Thus $n$ is bounded and $t$ fails for large $n$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-g4.title: Spiral similarity at $A_1$
imo-isl-2018-g4.body:
$\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ denotes the directed angle between lines, modulo $180^\circ$.

Let $CC_2$ meet $\Omega$ again at $K$ ($K=C_2$ if $CC_2$ is tangent). We show that $BB_2$ passes through $K$; by the same argument with $A$ in place of $B$, $AA_2$ passes through $K$ as well, which proves the statement. Since $K$, $B_2$, $C_2$, $A_1\in\Omega$, we have $\measuredangle(C_2K,C_2A_1)=\measuredangle(B_2K,B_2A_1)$, so it suffices to prove
$$\measuredangle(C_2C,C_2A_1)=\measuredangle(B_2B,B_2A_1).\qquad(1)$$
(Then the lines $B_2K$ and $B_2B$ make the same angle with $B_2A_1$, so they coincide.)

**Step 1.** $CB$ and $CA$ are the perpendicular bisectors of $TA_1$ and $TB_1$, so $CA_1=CT=CB_1$: $C$ is the circumcentre of $A_1TB_1$, and $CB$ bisects the angle $A_1CT$. By the inscribed angle theorem,
$$\measuredangle(CA_1,CB)=\measuredangle(CB,CT)=\measuredangle(B_1A_1,B_1T)=\measuredangle(B_1A_1,B_1B_2),$$
using that $B_2$ lies on line $B_1T$. In $\Omega$, $\measuredangle(B_1A_1,B_1B_2)=\measuredangle(C_2A_1,C_2B_2)$. Therefore
$$\measuredangle(CA_1,CB)=\measuredangle(C_2A_1,C_2B_2).\qquad(2)$$
Symmetrically (with $B$ the circumcentre of $A_1TC_1$),
$$\measuredangle(BA_1,BC)=\measuredangle(C_1A_1,C_1C_2)=\measuredangle(B_2A_1,B_2C_2).\qquad(3)$$

**Step 2.** By (2) and (3) the triangles $A_1BC$ and $A_1B_2C_2$ have equal directed angles at $C,C_2$ and at $B,B_2$, so they are similar with the same orientation. Hence
$$\frac{A_1B_2}{A_1B}=\frac{A_1C_2}{A_1C},\qquad \measuredangle(A_1B,A_1C)=\measuredangle(A_1B_2,A_1C_2).$$
The second equality is equivalent to $\measuredangle(A_1B,A_1B_2)=\measuredangle(A_1C,A_1C_2)$, and together with $A_1B:A_1B_2=A_1C:A_1C_2$ this shows that the triangles $A_1BB_2$ and $A_1CC_2$ are similar with the same orientation (spiral similarity at $A_1$). Comparing the angles at $B_2$ and $C_2$ gives exactly (1). ∎

imo-isl-2018-g5.title: Reflections of $\ell$ and a homothety
imo-isl-2018-g5.body:
$\measuredangle(m,n)$ denotes directed angles between lines modulo $180^\circ$. Let $X=y\cap z$, $Y=z\cap x$, $Z=x\cap y$, let $\Omega$ be the circle $XYZ$, and let $X_0,Y_0,Z_0$ be the second intersections of $AI,BI,CI$ with $\omega$.

**Preamble.** By the incentre–excentre lemma $Y_0A=Y_0I$ and $Z_0A=Z_0I$, so $Y_0Z_0$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AI$; it is perpendicular to $AI$, as is $x$ (perpendicular bisector of $AD$, with $D$ on $AI$). So $Y_0Z_0\parallel YZ$, and similarly $Z_0X_0\parallel ZX$, $X_0Y_0\parallel XY$. We will find a point $T\in\omega$ lying on the lines $XX_0$, $YY_0$, $ZZ_0$, and conclude from that.

Two useful identities (with $BI,CI,AI$ the angle bisectors): $2\measuredangle(BI,CI)=\measuredangle(BA,CA)$, $2\measuredangle(AI,BI)=\measuredangle(AC,BC)$, etc. (e.g. $2\measuredangle(BI,CI)=2\measuredangle(BI,BC)+2\measuredangle(BC,CI)=\measuredangle(BA,BC)+\measuredangle(BC,CA)$), and $\measuredangle(BI,CI)+90^\circ=\measuredangle(BA,AI)$ (the directed form of $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac12\angle A$).

**Claim 1.** The reflections $\ell_a,\ell_b,\ell_c$ of $\ell$ in $x,y,z$ pass through one point $T\in\omega$.

*Proof.* $\measuredangle(\ell_b,\ell_c)=\measuredangle(\ell_b,\ell)+\measuredangle(\ell,\ell_c)=2\measuredangle(y,\ell)+2\measuredangle(\ell,z)=2\measuredangle(y,z)$, and since $y\perp BI$, $z\perp CI$, this is $2\measuredangle(BI,CI)=\measuredangle(BA,CA)$:
$$\measuredangle(\ell_b,\ell_c)=\measuredangle(BA,CA),\qquad\text{similarly}\qquad\measuredangle(\ell_a,\ell_b)=\measuredangle(AC,BC).\qquad(1)$$
$A$ is the reflection of $D\in\ell$ in $x$, so $A\in\ell_a$; likewise $B\in\ell_b$, $C\in\ell_c$. So for $T'=\ell_a\cap\ell_b$, (1) gives $\measuredangle(T'A,T'B)=\measuredangle(CA,CB)$, hence $T'\in\omega$; similarly $T''=\ell_b\cap\ell_c\in\omega$. Both lie on $\ell_b\cap\omega$, which consists of $B$ and one more point. If $B\notin\ell_a$ and $B\notin\ell_c$, then $T',T''\ne B$, so $T'=T''$. If, say, $B\in\ell_c$, then $\ell_c=BC$ and (1) says $\measuredangle(\ell_b,BC)=\measuredangle(BA,CA)$, i.e. $\ell_b$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $B$, so $T'=T''=B$. (The case $B\in\ell_a$ is the same.) $\square$

**Claim 2.** $X$, $X_0$, $T$ are collinear (and likewise $Y,Y_0,T$ and $Z,Z_0,T$).

*Proof.* Let $D_b,D_c$ be the reflections of $D$ in $y,z$; then $D_b\in\ell_b$, $D_c\in\ell_c$, and $XD_b=XD=XD_c$ since $X\in y\cap z$. Also
$$\measuredangle(XD_b,XD_c)=2\measuredangle(y,XD)+2\measuredangle(XD,z)=2\measuredangle(y,z)=\measuredangle(\ell_b,\ell_c)=\measuredangle(TD_b,TD_c),$$
so $X,D_b,T,D_c$ are concyclic. In the circle with centre $X$ through $D,D_b,D_c$, the angle between the chord $D_bD_c$ and the radius $D_cX$ is $\measuredangle(D_bD_c,D_cX)=90^\circ+\measuredangle(DD_b,DD_c)$. As $DD_b\perp y\perp BI$ and $DD_c\perp z\perp CI$, $\measuredangle(DD_b,DD_c)=\measuredangle(BI,CI)$. Hence
$$\measuredangle(\ell_b,XT)=\measuredangle(D_bT,XT)=\measuredangle(D_bD_c,D_cX)=90^\circ+\measuredangle(BI,CI)=\measuredangle(BA,AI)=\measuredangle(BA,AX_0)=\measuredangle(BT,TX_0)=\measuredangle(\ell_b,X_0T),$$
using the cyclic quadrilateral $XD_bTD_c$, and then $A,B,T,X_0\in\omega$. So the lines $XT$ and $X_0T$ coincide. $\square$

**Conclusion.** The map sending $X_0Y_0Z_0$ to $XYZ$ (corresponding sides parallel) is a homothety or a translation. It is not the identity (otherwise $x=Y_0Z_0$, forcing $D=I$). A translation by a vector $v\ne0$ is impossible: the lines $XX_0,YY_0,ZZ_0$ would be three parallel lines through $T$, i.e. one line containing $X,Y,Z$, but $XYZ$ is a genuine triangle. So it is a homothety $h$ with some centre $O$. If $O\ne T$, every line $XX_0$, $YY_0$, $ZZ_0$ (or the point $X_0=X=O$ if they coincide) lies on line $OT$, which would make the three distinct points $X_0,Y_0,Z_0$ of $\omega$ collinear — impossible. So $h$ has centre $T$. Then $h(\omega)=\Omega$ and $T=h(T)\in\Omega$; the tangent to $\omega$ at $T$ is mapped to a parallel line through $T$, namely the tangent to $\Omega$ at $T$. So $\omega$ and $\Omega$ are tangent at $T$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-g7.title: Concyclic points and a tangent–chord angle
imo-isl-2018-g7.body:
$\measuredangle(a,b)$ is the directed angle between lines modulo $180^\circ$; we often use that $a_1\perp a_2$, $b_1\perp b_2$ imply $\measuredangle(a_1,b_1)=\measuredangle(a_2,b_2)$.

Let $L_A=\ell_B\cap\ell_C$, $L_B=\ell_C\cap\ell_A$, $L_C=\ell_A\cap\ell_B$. The sides of $L_AL_BL_C$ are perpendicular to those of $ABC$, and $O_A\in\ell_A=L_BL_C$, etc. The points $O_A,O_B,O_C$ all lie on the perpendicular bisector $m$ of $OP$. Moreover, $OO_A$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AP$ (both $O$ and $O_A$ are equidistant from $A$ and $P$), so $OO_A\perp AP$; similarly $OO_B\perp BP$, $OO_C\perp CP$.

**Claim 1.** $L_B,P,O_A,O_C$ are concyclic.

*Proof.* $P$ is the reflection of $O$ in $m=O_AO_C$, so
$$\measuredangle(O_AP,O_CP)=\measuredangle(O_CO,O_AO)=\measuredangle(CP,AP)=\measuredangle(CB,AB)=\measuredangle(\ell_A,\ell_C)=\measuredangle(O_AL_B,O_CL_B),$$
using $OO_C\perp CP$, $OO_A\perp AP$, then $P\in\Omega$, then $\ell_A\perp BC$, $\ell_C\perp AB$. $\square$

Call this circle $\omega_B$, and define $\omega_A$ (through $L_A,P,O_B,O_C$) and $\omega_C$ (through $L_C,P,O_A,O_B$) in the same way.

**Claim 2.** $P$ lies on the circle $L_AL_BL_C$.

*Proof.* Using $\omega_C$, then $O_B,O_C\in m$, then $\omega_B$:
$$\measuredangle(L_CL_A,L_CP)=\measuredangle(L_CO_B,L_CP)=\measuredangle(O_AO_B,O_AP)=\measuredangle(O_AO_C,O_AP)=\measuredangle(L_BO_C,L_BP)=\measuredangle(L_BL_A,L_BP).\ \square$$

**Claim 3.** $P$, $L_C$, $C$ are collinear.

*Proof.* By $\omega_C$, $\measuredangle(PL_C,L_CL_A)=\measuredangle(PL_C,L_CO_B)=\measuredangle(PO_A,O_AO_B)$. Since $O_A$ is the centre of the circle $AOP$ and $O_AO_B$ is the perpendicular bisector of its chord $OP$, the inscribed angle theorem gives $\measuredangle(PO_A,O_AO_B)=\measuredangle(PA,AO)$. As $O$ is the centre of the circle $PCA$, $\measuredangle(PA,AO)=90^\circ-\measuredangle(CA,CP)$ (angle between a chord and a radius). Finally $L_CL_A=\ell_B\perp CA$, so $\measuredangle(CP,L_CL_A)=\measuredangle(CP,CA)+90^\circ$, which is the same. Hence
$$\measuredangle(PL_C,L_CL_A)=\measuredangle(PA,AO)=\measuredangle(CP,L_CL_A),\qquad(*)$$
so the lines $PL_C$ and $CP$ are parallel; both pass through $P$, so they coincide. $\square$

In the same way (permuting letters), $P$, $L_A$, $A$ are collinear.

**Tangency.** Triangle $OPA$ is isosceles ($OP=OA$), so $\measuredangle(OP,PA)=\measuredangle(PA,AO)$. With $PA=PL_A$ and $(*)$,
$$\measuredangle(OP,PL_A)=\measuredangle(PA,AO)=\measuredangle(L_CP,L_CL_A).$$
By Claim 2, $P,L_A,L_C$ lie on the circle $L_AL_BL_C$, and this equality is the tangent–chord condition: $OP$ is tangent to that circle at $P$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-n1.title: Divisibility kills it; otherwise tune exponents
imo-isl-2018-n1.body:
**Answer: all pairs $(n,k)$ with $n\nmid k$ and $k\nmid n$.**

Let $d(m)$ be the number of divisors; for $m=\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$, $d(m)=\prod(\alpha_i+1)$.

**If $n\mid k$ (with $n\ne k$), no $s$ works.** For any $s$, $sn\mid sk$ and $sn<sk$, so every divisor of $sn$ divides $sk$, while $sk$ itself does not divide $sn$. Hence $d(sn)<d(sk)$. The case $k\mid n$ is symmetric.

**If $n\nmid k$ and $k\nmid n$, a suitable $s$ exists.** Let $p_1,\dots,p_t$ be the primes dividing $nk$, $n=\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$, $k=\prod p_i^{\beta_i}$, and look for $s=\prod p_i^{\gamma_i}$. Then
$$\frac{d(sn)}{d(sk)}=\prod_{i=1}^t\frac{\alpha_i+\gamma_i+1}{\beta_i+\gamma_i+1}.$$
Indices with $\alpha_i=\beta_i$ contribute $1$ whatever $\gamma_i$ is (take $\gamma_i=0$), so ignore them and renumber the remaining $t$ primes so that $\alpha_i>\beta_i$ for $i\le u$ and $\alpha_i<\beta_i$ for $i>u$. Since $n\nmid k$ and $k\nmid n$, $1\le u\le t-1$.

*Lemma.* If $\alpha>\beta\ge0$ are integers and $M\ge\beta+1$, there is an integer $\gamma\ge0$ with $\frac{\alpha+\gamma+1}{\beta+\gamma+1}=\frac{M+1}M$.

*Proof.* The equation is $\frac{\alpha-\beta}{\beta+\gamma+1}=\frac1M$, i.e. $\gamma=M(\alpha-\beta)-(\beta+1)\ge M-\beta-1\ge0$. $\square$

Choose an integer $X$ larger than all $\alpha_i,\beta_i$. By the lemma pick the $\gamma_i$ so that
$$\frac{\alpha_i+\gamma_i+1}{\beta_i+\gamma_i+1}=\frac{uX+i}{uX+i-1}\ \ (1\le i\le u),\qquad \frac{\beta_{u+i}+\gamma_{u+i}+1}{\alpha_{u+i}+\gamma_{u+i}+1}=\frac{(t-u)X+i}{(t-u)X+i-1}\ \ (1\le i\le t-u)$$
(here $M=uX+i-1\ge X>\beta_i$, resp. $M=(t-u)X+i-1\ge X>\alpha_{u+i}$). The products telescope:
$$\frac{d(sn)}{d(sk)}=\prod_{i=1}^u\frac{uX+i}{uX+i-1}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{t-u}\frac{(t-u)X+i-1}{(t-u)X+i}=\frac{u(X+1)}{uX}\cdot\frac{(t-u)X}{(t-u)(X+1)}=1.$$
So $d(sn)=d(sk)$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-n2.title: Both sums equal $n-1+P$
imo-isl-2018-n2.body:
Let $A_{ij}$ be the entries, $a_{ij}=A_{ij}-1$, and let $P$ be the product of all $n^2$ entries. We show
$$\sum_{i=1}^nR_i\equiv(n-1)+P\pmod{n^4}.\qquad(1)$$
The conditions are symmetric in rows and columns, so the same holds for $\sum C_j$, and the two sums are congruent modulo $n^4$.

By (i), $n\mid a_{ij}$ for all $i,j$, so every product of two or more of the $a_{ij}$ is divisible by $n^2$. Expanding,
$$R_i=\prod_{j=1}^n(1+a_{ij})\equiv1+\sum_{j=1}^na_{ij}=1-n+\sum_{j=1}^nA_{ij}\pmod{n^2}.$$
By (ii), $\sum_jA_{ij}\equiv n\pmod{n^2}$, hence $R_i\equiv1\pmod{n^2}$. Write $r_i=R_i-1$; then $n^2\mid r_i$, so every product of two or more $r_i$ is divisible by $n^4$, and
$$P=\prod_{i=1}^nR_i=\prod_{i=1}^n(1+r_i)\equiv1+\sum_{i=1}^nr_i\pmod{n^4}.$$
Therefore $\sum R_i=n+\sum r_i\equiv n+(P-1)\pmod{n^4}$, which is (1). ∎

imo-isl-2018-n3.title: Complements inside partial sums
imo-isl-2018-n3.body:
Call a nonnegative integer *representable* if it is a sum of distinct terms of the sequence (zero or one term allowed), and write $b\sim c$ if $b,c$ are both representable or both not. Note $a_0<a_1<a_2<\dots$ ($2,3,6,10,20,36,72,136,\dots$).

**Partial sums.** $S_{n-1}:=a_0+\dots+a_{n-1}=2^n+2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}+2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}-3$. This holds for $n=1$ ($S_0=2$), and $S_n-S_{n-1}=2^n+2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1}-2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=a_n$ because $\{\lceil\frac{n+1}2\rceil,\lfloor\frac{n+1}2\rfloor\}=\{\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor+1,\lceil\frac n2\rceil\}$. Hence
$$S_{n-1}-a_n=2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}-3,$$
which for $n\ge3$ is positive and less than $a_n$.

**Claim 1.** If $S_{n-1}-a_n<b<a_n$ for some $n\ge3$, then $b\sim S_{n-1}-b$.

*Proof.* Put $c=S_{n-1}-b$; then also $S_{n-1}-a_n<c<a_n$, so the situation is symmetric. If $b$ is representable, its representation uses only terms smaller than $a_n$, i.e. a subset of $\{a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\}$, and then $c$ is the sum of the complementary subset. $\square$

**Claim 2.** For $n\ge3$, $a_n$ is a sum of two or more distinct terms iff $2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}-3$ is representable.

*Proof.* Let $c=S_{n-1}-a_n=2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}-3<a_n$. If $a_n$ is such a sum, the terms used are among $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$, and $c$ is the sum of the others. Conversely, a representation of $c$ uses terms among $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$, and the complementary terms sum to $a_n$; there are at least two of them, since the sum $a_n$ is neither $0$ nor a single earlier term. $\square$

Taking $n=2t$, it therefore suffices to find infinitely many representable numbers of the form $2^t-3$ and infinitely many non-representable ones.

**Claim 3.** For $t\ge3$: $2^t-3\sim2^{4t-6}-3$, and $4t-6>t$.

*Proof.* With $n=2t-2\ge4$: $S_{2t-3}=2^{2t-2}+2^t-3$ and $S_{2t-3}-a_{2t-2}=2^{t-1}-3<2^t-3<2^{2t-2}<a_{2t-2}$, so by Claim 1, $2^t-3\sim S_{2t-3}-(2^t-3)=2^{2t-2}$. With $n=4t-6\ge6$: $S_{4t-7}=2^{4t-6}+2^{2t-2}-3$ and $S_{4t-7}-a_{4t-6}=2^{2t-3}-3<2^{2t-2}<a_{4t-6}$, so $2^{2t-2}\sim S_{4t-7}-2^{2t-2}=2^{4t-6}-3$. $\square$

**Starting values.** $2^3-3=5=a_0+a_1$ is representable, so Claim 3 gives the representable numbers $2^t-3$ for $t=3,6,18,66,\dots$. And $2^7-3=125$ is not: by Claim 1, $125\sim S_6-125=24$ (as $13<125<136=a_7$), $24\sim S_4-24=17$ (as $5<24<36=a_5$), $17\sim S_3-17=4$ (as $1<17<20=a_4$), and $4$ is clearly not a sum of distinct terms of $2,3,6,\dots$. So Claim 3 gives non-representable $2^t-3$ for $t=7,22,82,\dots$.

By Claim 2 (with $n=2t$), infinitely many $a_n$ are sums of two or more distinct terms and infinitely many are not. ∎

imo-isl-2018-n5.title: Sums of two squares
imo-isl-2018-n5.body:
**Answer: No.**

Suppose $xy=a^2$ and $zt=c^2$ with $a,c>0$.

If $x+y=z+t$ were odd, then $x,y$ would have opposite parities, and so would $z,t$; then $xy$ and $zt$ would both be even, and so would $xy-zt=x+y$ — a contradiction. So $s=\frac{x+y}2=\frac{z+t}2$ is a positive integer. Let $b=\frac{|x-y|}2$ and $d=\frac{|z-t|}2$ (nonnegative integers). Since $\{x,y\}=\{s+b,s-b\}$ and $\{z,t\}=\{s+d,s-d\}$,
$$s^2=a^2+b^2=c^2+d^2,\qquad(1)$$
$$2s=a^2-c^2=d^2-b^2,\qquad(2)$$
where the second equality in (2) follows from (1). In particular $a>c$ and $d>b$, so $d>0$.

Relations (1), (2) are unchanged by the swap $a\leftrightarrow d$, $b\leftrightarrow c$, so we may assume $b\ge c$; then $b\ge c>0$. Now $d^2=2s+b^2>c^2$, so by (1)
$$d^2>\frac{c^2+d^2}2=\frac{s^2}2.\qquad(3)$$
By (2), $d^2-b^2$ is even, so $b\equiv d\pmod 2$, and with $0<b<d$ we get $b\le d-2$. Hence
$$2s=d^2-b^2\ge d^2-(d-2)^2=4(d-1),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad d\le\frac s2+1.\qquad(4)$$
From (3) and (4), $2s^2<4d^2\le(s+2)^2$, i.e. $(s-2)^2<8$, so $s\le4$. But none of $1,4,9,16$ is a sum of two **positive** squares, while (1) says $s^2=a^2+b^2$ with $a,b>0$. Contradiction.

So $xy$ and $zt$ cannot both be perfect squares.

imo-isl-2018-n6.title: Sets of indices where $m$ divides $f$
imo-isl-2018-n6.body:
For a positive integer $m$ let $S_m=\{n\ge1:\ m\mid f(n)\}$.

**Lemma.** If $S_m$ is infinite, then $S_m=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$ where $d=\min S_m$.

*Proof.* We have $m\mid f(d)$. If $n\in S_m$ and $n>d$, then $m\mid f(n)\mid f(n-d)+f(d)$, so $m\mid f(n-d)$ and $n-d\in S_m$. Repeating, all of $n-d,n-2d,\dots$ down to the number $r\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ with $r\equiv n\pmod d$ lie in $S_m$; by minimality of $d$, $r=d$, so $d\mid n$. Thus $S_m$ consists of multiples of $d$; and starting from arbitrarily large elements of $S_m$ and stepping down by $d$ we reach every multiple of $d$, so all of them are in $S_m$. $\square$

**Case 1: $f$ is bounded.** Then only finitely many primes divide some value of $f$. Call a prime $p$ *frequent* if $S_p$ is infinite and *sporadic* otherwise. Only finitely many $n$ have $f(n)$ divisible by a sporadic prime; let $N$ exceed all of them. Let $p_1,\dots,p_k$ be the frequent primes and, by the lemma, $S_{p_i}=d_i\mathbb Z_{>0}$. Put $n=Nd_1d_2\cdots d_k+1>N$. Since $f(n)\ge2$, it has a prime divisor, which is frequent (as $n>N$), say $p_i$. Then $n\in S_{p_i}$, so $d_i\mid n$; but $n\equiv1\pmod{d_i}$, hence $d_i=1$ and $S_{p_i}$ is everything: $c=p_i$ divides all values of $f$.

**Case 2: $f$ is unbounded.** Let $a=f(1)\ge2$; we show $a$ divides every value. Since $1\in S_a$, by the lemma it suffices to show that $S_a$ is infinite (then $\min S_a=1$).

Call $p$ a *peak* if $f(p)>\max(f(1),\dots,f(p-1))$. As $f$ is unbounded there are infinitely many peaks $p_1<p_2<\dots$; let $h_i=f(p_i)$. For a peak $p_i$ and $1\le k<p_i$, $f(p_i)\mid f(k)+f(p_i-k)$ and $0<f(k)+f(p_i-k)<2f(p_i)$, so
$$f(k)+f(p_i-k)=f(p_i)=h_i.\qquad(1)$$
By pigeonhole, infinitely many $h_i$ are congruent modulo $a$: say $h_{k_0}\equiv h_{k_1}\equiv\dots$ with $k_0<k_1<\dots$. By (1) with $k=p_{k_0}<p_{k_i}$,
$$f(p_{k_i}-p_{k_0})=h_{k_i}-h_{k_0}\equiv0\pmod a,$$
so $p_{k_i}-p_{k_0}\in S_a$ for all $i\ge1$: infinitely many elements. Hence $c=f(1)$ divides every value of $f$. ∎

imo-isl-2018-n7.title: Too many denominators divisible by $d$
imo-isl-2018-n7.body:
Suppose the progression has nonzero difference $\Delta=\frac cd$ with $d>0$ and $\gcd(c,d)=1$. For a prime $p\mid d$, call an index $i$ *$p$-wrong* if $v_p(b_i)<v_p(d)$ ($v_p$ = exponent of $p$).

**Claim 1.** All $p$-wrong indices are congruent modulo $p$.

*Proof.* Let $\alpha=v_p(d)\ge1$, and let $i,j$ be $p$-wrong with $i\not\equiv j\pmod p$. The difference $\frac{a_i}{b_i}-\frac{a_j}{b_j}$ can be written with denominator $\operatorname{lcm}(b_i,b_j)$, which is not divisible by $p^\alpha$. But it equals $\frac{(i-j)c}d$, and $p\nmid(i-j)c$, so in lowest terms its denominator is divisible by $p^\alpha$. Contradiction. $\square$

**Claim 2.** $d$ has no prime divisor $p\ge7$.

*Proof.* By Claim 1 at most $\lceil n/p\rceil<\frac np+1$ indices are $p$-wrong, so $p\mid b_i$ for more than $\frac{p-1}pn-1$ indices. These $b_i$ are distinct multiples of $p$, so the largest is at least
$$p\Big(\frac{p-1}pn-1\Big)=(p-1)(n-1)-1\ge6(n-1)-1>5n,$$
contradicting $b_i\le5n$. $\square$

**Claim 3.** Among any $30$ consecutive indices $k+1,\dots,k+30$, at least $8$ satisfy $d\mid b_i$.

*Proof.* By Claims 1 and 2, all wrong indices lie in one residue class mod $2$, one mod $3$ and one mod $5$ (for primes not dividing $d$ there are none). By the Chinese remainder theorem, exactly $(2-1)(3-1)(5-1)=8$ of the $30$ consecutive indices avoid all three classes. Such an index $i$ is not $p$-wrong for any $p\mid d$, i.e. $v_p(b_i)\ge v_p(d)$ for all $p$, so $d\mid b_i$. $\square$

**Claim 4.** $|\Delta|<\frac{20}{n-2}$, hence $d>\frac{n-2}{20}$.

*Proof.* Fewer than $\frac n2$ of the distinct $b_i$ are less than $\frac n2$. The remaining at least $\frac n2$ fractions satisfy $0<\frac{a_i}{b_i}\le\frac{5n}{n/2}=10$. So at least $\frac n2$ distinct terms of the progression lie in $(0,10]$, which forces $(\frac n2-1)|\Delta|<10$, i.e. $|\Delta|<\frac{20}{n-2}$. As $c$ is a nonzero integer, $\frac1d\le\frac{|c|}d=|\Delta|$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** Splitting $1,\dots,n$ into $\lfloor n/30\rfloor$ disjoint blocks of $30$, Claim 3 gives at least $8\lfloor n/30\rfloor$ indices with $d\mid b_i$; these $b_i$ are distinct multiples of $d$, so by Claim 4
$$5n\ge\max_{d\mid b_i}b_i\ge8\Big\lfloor\frac n{30}\Big\rfloor d>8\Big(\frac n{30}-1\Big)\frac{n-2}{20}=\frac{(n-30)(n-2)}{75}.$$
For $n\ge2018$ the right side exceeds $5n$ (e.g. $(n-30)(n-2)\ge1988\,(n-2)>375n$). This contradiction shows $\Delta=0$: all terms are equal. ∎
